intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note says what a slide is for, how to hold it in memory and where practitioners slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the recall questions, and add your own district's numbers beside the examples.

sections.title: Why Maternal Health Matters
sections.big_idea: A maternal death is a death that care already known could almost always prevent. **Check the definition and the denominator** before you compare any two numbers.
in_plain_words: A maternal death is a death during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end, from a cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy. The 42-day line is a convention with no clinical basis, and widening it raises the count without one extra death. The ratio (MMR) divides deaths by 100,000 live births, the rate divides by women aged 15 to 49, and lifetime risk is cumulative per woman.

The deck frames maternal health as a rights issue, with Indian courts treating denial of care as a breach of Article 21. SDG 3.1 sets a global target below 70 by 2030 and a national floor of 140, with nothing at state or district level. The remedies are old and cheap, so the failure lies in delivery, and the burden falls hardest on the poorest places.

diagram.note: the ratio answers how dangerous one pregnancy is in this place

key_terms.meaning: Death in pregnancy or within 42 days of its end, from a pregnancy-related cause.
The same kind of death, 42 days to one year after the pregnancy.
Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
Cumulative risk across a woman's whole reproductive life.
Global MMR below 70 by 2030, with no country above 140.
Enforceable in court; the deck says the right to maternal care is.

worked_example.title: Calculate an MMR and read it against SDG 3.1
worked_example.setup: An illustrative district records 24 maternal deaths and 30,000 live births in a year.
steps: Distance above the global target of 70: 80 − 70 = 10.
Distance below the national floor of 140: 140 − 80 = 60.
Read it plainly: the district meets the floor and misses the global target, and with only 24 deaths a single case moves the ratio a lot.
worked_example.answer: An MMR of 80 per 100,000 live births, 10 above the global target and 60 below the national floor.

mistakes: Comparing two countries' maternal mortality figures without checking the 42-day definition behind each.
Using 'maternal mortality rate' and 'ratio' as if they were one measure. The denominators differ.
Treating a good national MMR as success when states and districts can sit far above the target.
Describing maternal death as a tragedy only, which leaves out the duty-bearer who failed.

recall.q: What is the denominator of the MMR?
recall.a: 100,000 live births.

recall.q: What distinguishes a late maternal death?
recall.a: It occurs between 42 days and one year after the pregnancy ends.

recall.q: What does SDG 3.1 set as the global MMR target?
recall.a: Below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030.

recall.q: What is the national floor in SDG 3.1?
recall.a: No country above 140, twice the global target.

recall.q: Which constitutional article have Indian courts used for denial of maternal care?
recall.a: Article 21, the right to life.

sections.title: Why Mothers Die
sections.big_idea: Five direct causes and one great indirect cause explain most deaths. **Anaemia turns survivable events into deaths**, and the dangerous hours are few.
in_plain_words: Direct causes arise from the pregnancy or its treatment: haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders and eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion. Globally haemorrhage is about a quarter, hypertensive disorders roughly one in seven, sepsis about one in ten and unsafe abortion close to one in twelve. Each has a cheap remedy that is decades old.

Indirect causes are conditions the pregnancy worsens, such as anaemia, heart disease, TB and diabetes. As direct deaths fall, indirect causes take a larger share. In India about 52% of pregnant women were anaemic in NFHS-5. Most deaths cluster around labour and the first 24 hours after birth, so **the risk is concentrated in hours** while services are organised in days.

left.title: Direct causes
items: From the pregnancy or its management
Respond to obstetric care at the right moment

right.title: Indirect causes
items: Respond to care across the life course
Become the larger share of what remains

key_terms.meaning: Postpartum haemorrhage: severe bleeding after delivery, the leading direct cause.
High blood pressure with protein in the urine; can progress to eclampsia.
Convulsions in a woman with pre-eclampsia.
A serious infection of the genital tract after childbirth or abortion.
A lasting injury from obstructed labour that leaves a woman incontinent.
Too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen; the great indirect killer.

worked_example.title: Turn global shares into counts
worked_example.setup: Take 1,000 direct maternal deaths and the deck's approximate global shares (a quarter, one in seven, one in ten, one in twelve). The shares are illustrative for any one country.
worked_example.answer: About 576 of 1,000 deaths come from the four named causes, so plan from your own district's death review data.

mistakes: Planning a district programme from a global cause distribution when shares vary widely by country.
Looking for anaemia on the death certificate. It rarely appears as the certified cause but sits behind many deaths.
Reassuring a woman at sepsis risk because she went home well, when sepsis can present on day three.
Treating unsafe abortion as a medical mystery when legal, safe services eliminate it.

recall.q: What is the largest single direct cause of maternal death?
recall.a: Haemorrhage, about a quarter globally.

recall.q: Which drug controls and prevents eclampsia seizures?
recall.a: Magnesium sulphate.

recall.q: Name the six cleans of safe delivery.
recall.a: Clean hands, delivery surface, blade, cord tie, cord stump and perineum.

recall.q: What share of pregnant women in India was anaemic in NFHS-5?
recall.a: About 52%.

recall.q: Why does the most dangerous window matter for planning?
recall.a: Deaths cluster in labour and the first 24 hours, so an attendant at birth and a working referral come first.

sections.title: The Three Delays
sections.big_idea: The clinical cause is the last step. **Where did the time go** is the better question, and each delay has a different owner.
in_plain_words: Thaddeus and Maine (1994) described three delays: in deciding to seek care, in reaching a facility and in receiving adequate care once there. A death usually reflects more than one. The model reframes maternal death from a medical event into a systems failure that spans the household, the road and the hospital.

Each delay has different causes, remedies and owners. Delay one stalls on unknown danger signs, cost, fear and who decides, and a trusted ASHA shifts it more than a poster. Delay two needs night dispatch, free referral transport and birth-waiting homes. Delay three covers staff, drugs, blood, the anaesthetist and paperwork. **Fixing one delay can move deaths to another**, so the three move together.

diagram.caption: the path from complication to outcome, with three places to intervene

key_terms.meaning: Deciding, reaching and receiving care; the model of Thaddeus and Maine, 1994.
Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram: free delivery, drugs, blood and transport, from 2011.
Ambulance dispatch numbers for referral transport.
A residence near the referral facility for women from remote areas.
A structured interview with family to reconstruct how a death unfolded.
Maternal Death Surveillance and Response, a no-blame review of every death.

worked_example.title: Where did the time go?
worked_example.setup: An illustrative death review finds the family took 3 hours to decide to leave, the journey took 2 hours and the woman waited 1 hour for first treatment.
steps: Half the time sat at home, so the owners to engage first are the ASHA, the community and the woman's family.
worked_example.answer: Half the elapsed time was Delay 1, so training clinicians alone (Delay 3) would not have saved her.

mistakes: Training clinicians when women are dying at delay one, before they ever reach a facility.
Measuring ambulance fleet size when the question is the response on the worst night of last year.
Funding a cash incentive that delivers women to labour rooms that are not ready.
Running a death review that ends in suspensions, which stops deaths being reported.

recall.q: Who proposed the three delays model, and when?
recall.a: Thaddeus and Maine, in 1994.

recall.q: Which delay does the anaesthetist problem belong to?
recall.a: Delay 3, receiving adequate care.

recall.q: What fixes Delay 2 at night?
recall.a: A dispatch system that answers at night (102 / 108) and free referral transport.

recall.q: Why is the second referral the one that kills?
recall.a: The woman has spent her margin on a journey to a facility that could not manage her.

recall.q: Why must demand-side and supply-side investment move together?
recall.a: Otherwise the second delay simply becomes the third.

sections.title: The Continuum of Care
sections.big_idea: Care is a chain over time and place. **Women fall out at the handovers**, which routine coverage figures do not count.
in_plain_words: The continuum runs from before pregnancy through antenatal care, skilled birth, postnatal care and the newborn, and from home and community to facility. A break anywhere puts mother and baby at risk. The stages are not substitutes: excellent antenatal care does not make up for an unattended birth, because each manages different risks.

Coverage figures measure services, while women die at the joins. Four stages at 80% coverage can mean 80% of women received everything, or a large group received nothing. Name-based tracking in RCH and HMIS tells these apart. The frontline team runs from ASHA to specialist, and **the ASHA is the only member without a salary**, so any added duty is unpaid work on the busiest link.

diagram.caption: referral tiers, top first: each refers up what it cannot manage

key_terms.meaning: Linked care across time (pre-pregnancy to childhood) and place (home to facility).
The join between stages or levels where women fall out of the system.
First Referral Unit: round-the-clock caesarean, blood and newborn care.
Accredited Social Health Activist, the village-level link to the health system.
Mother and Child Protection Card, a record the woman holds.
Health and wellness centre, the upgraded sub-centre.

worked_example.title: Measure continuum completion
worked_example.setup: An illustrative district counts 1,000 women who delivered. Of them, 800 attended four ANC visits, and 560 of those 800 had a postnatal contact within 48 hours.
steps: Drop between the two coverage figures: 80 − 56 = 24 points.
worked_example.answer: Only 56% of women completed both stages, a drop of 24 points from the ANC figure alone.

mistakes: Reporting each stage's coverage and assuming the same women received every stage.
Calling a facility an FRU because it is designated, when it has no anaesthetist at night.
Adding duties to ASHAs without payment, which makes pilots fail at scale.
Skipping the newborn, who in many deliveries is never separately examined.

recall.q: What are the four core stages of the continuum?
recall.a: Antenatal, skilled birth, postnatal and newborn care.

recall.q: What is the UN benchmark for EmONC facilities?
recall.a: At least five per 500,000 population, of which at least one can do surgery and transfusion (CEmONC).

recall.q: Which instrument links stages and places in the record a woman holds?
recall.a: The Mother and Child Protection Card.

recall.q: What does a time gap need compared with a place gap?
recall.a: A time gap needs outreach and follow-up; a place gap needs transport, communication and a prepared receiving facility.

recall.q: How is the ASHA paid?
recall.a: Task-based incentives per activity completed, and she is classified as a volunteer.

sections.title: Antenatal Care
sections.big_idea: Antenatal care converts silent risks into managed ones. **It is a set of tests and counselling**, and attendance alone shows none of it.
in_plain_words: ANC finds raised blood pressure and protein in urine, low haemoglobin, malpresentation, infections and gestational diabetes before they become emergencies. A visit that records weight and hands over tablets is not ANC; the BP cuff, the haemoglobin test and the urine dipstick are what the visit is for. In 2016 WHO moved from a minimum of 4 visits to a recommended 8 contacts, with the first before 12 weeks.

In NFHS-5 about 58% of mothers had four visits, and a much smaller minority had full ANC with IFA and tetanus protection. Anaemia affects about 52% of pregnant women. IFA works only when swallowed, and Anemia Mukt Bharat adds testing and deworming. Tetanus toxoid is a success: neonatal tetanus was eliminated as a public-health problem, validated in 2015.

key_terms.meaning: WHO 2016 term for an antenatal touchpoint; it can happen in the community.
Iron and folic acid supplements that raise haemoglobin.
Tetanus and diphtheria vaccine that replaced tetanus toxoid in pregnancy.
Warning signs such as bleeding, severe headache, fever and convulsions.
A fixed monthly day of free, quality antenatal check-ups with a specialist.
Four visits plus IFA and tetanus protection, all components together.

worked_example.title: Size the ANC gap in a block
worked_example.setup: An illustrative block has 2,000 mothers. Use the NFHS-5 shares from the deck: about 58% had at least four visits, and about 52% of pregnant women are anaemic.
steps: Mothers with four or more visits: 2,000 × 0.58 = 1,160.
Extra contacts if the WHO model were followed: 8 − 4 = 4 more per woman.
worked_example.answer: 840 mothers had fewer than four visits and about 1,040 were anaemic, so even full attendance would leave testing and treatment to be checked.

mistakes: Counting visits as antenatal care without checking BP, haemoglobin and urine protein were done.
Counting IFA tablets distributed as tablets swallowed, which is the figure that moves haemoglobin.
Teaching danger signs to the woman alone when someone else makes the decision.
Assuming iron closes every anaemia gap, when hookworm, malaria and haemoglobinopathies need other responses.

recall.q: What change did WHO make to antenatal care in 2016?
recall.a: It moved from a minimum of 4 visits to a recommended 8 contacts, with the first before 12 weeks.

recall.q: What share of mothers had four ANC visits in NFHS-5?
recall.a: About 58%.

recall.q: What does MgSO4 do?
recall.a: It prevents and controls eclamptic seizures.

recall.q: What does 'elimination' of neonatal tetanus mean?
recall.a: Fewer than one case per 1,000 live births per district; zero is not required.

recall.q: Which scheme gives a fixed monthly day of quality antenatal care?
recall.a: PMSMA.

sections.title: Skilled Birth & Institutional Delivery
sections.big_idea: A facility birth pre-pays the first two delays. **Cash gets women in, and quality decides** whether they live.
in_plain_words: A skilled birth attendant is an accredited doctor, nurse or midwife who manages normal birth and can recognise, manage or refer complications. Training traditional birth attendants did not reduce maternal mortality, because deaths need drugs, surgery and blood. A facility birth brings the woman to where those are, which turns a two-hour problem into a two-minute one.

India's institutional delivery rose from about 39% (NFHS-3) to 79% to 89% (NFHS-5). JSY (2005) pays a conditional cash incentive and JSSK (2011) removes charges, so one pulls women in and the other makes it free. The caveat is quality: **a crowded labour room with no drugs or skilled provider is a false promise**, and further decline depends on what happens inside facilities.

left.title: JSY (2005)
items: Addresses decision and cost of coming
Cannot buy quality once she is inside

right.title: JSSK (2011)
items: Removes costs incurred at the facility
Only as strong as her knowledge of it

key_terms.meaning: Skilled birth attendant: an accredited doctor, nurse or midwife.
Traditional birth attendant; training programmes did not cut maternal deaths.
Janani Suraksha Yojana: conditional cash for facility birth, from 2005.
Money to households to change behaviour, here facility birth.
A birth in a health facility.
Labour Room Quality Improvement initiative.

worked_example.title: Read the institutional-delivery surge
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS figures: about 39% in NFHS-3 (2005-06) and about 89% in NFHS-5 (2019-21).
steps: Ratio of the later share to the earlier: 89 ÷ 39 = 2.3.
Those 110 are concentrated among the poorest quintile, Adivasi communities and the remotest blocks.
worked_example.answer: A fifty-point rise, more than doubling the share, and about 110 of every 1,000 births still at home.

mistakes: Equating a facility birth with a safe birth when staff, drugs, blood and a theatre may be missing.
Reading JSY's success as proof that more cash would buy quality. Cash cannot supply an anaesthetist.
Assuming women know what is free under JSSK, when informal payments persist where they do not.
Treating the 89% national figure as universal when the remaining home births sit with the highest-mortality groups.

recall.q: What does JSY pay for?
recall.a: A cash incentive to give birth in a health facility, with an ASHA incentive for accompaniment.

recall.q: What does JSSK entitle every pregnant woman to?
recall.a: Free delivery including caesarean, drugs, diagnostics, blood, transport and diet in public facilities.

recall.q: What was institutional delivery in NFHS-3, NFHS-4 and NFHS-5?
recall.a: About 39%, 79% and 89%.

recall.q: Why did the training of traditional birth attendants fail to reduce deaths?
recall.a: The deaths need drugs, surgery and blood that training cannot supply.

recall.q: Which two programmes mark the shift from coverage to quality?
recall.a: LaQshya and SUMAN.

sections.title: Emergency Obstetric & Newborn Care
sections.big_idea: Risk screening cannot predict who will bleed. **Every birth needs reach to emergency care**, and readiness is only as strong as its weakest link.
in_plain_words: Most women who develop a complication have no known risk factor, so universal access to emergency care replaced risk screening as the standard. Basic EmONC has seven signal functions at PHC level, and the full level (CEmONC) adds caesarean and blood transfusion, for nine. A function never performed in the last three months counts as absent.

Referral has four steps: recognise early, stabilise before moving, transport and communicate ahead. The partograph plots labour against time with alert and action lines. Newborn resuscitation with bag and mask in the first minute saves babies who do not breathe. **Readiness is a conjunction, and a sum would mislead**: people, drugs, blood, theatre and transport must all be present on the worst shift.

key_terms.meaning: Emergency obstetric and newborn care, services that treat complications.
A life-saving service used to judge a facility's real capability.
Basic EmONC: seven signal functions, without surgery.
Adds caesarean section and blood transfusion to the basic seven.
A chart of labour progress with alert and action lines.
First-dose treatment, such as MgSO4, given before moving a woman.

worked_example.title: Check a district against the EmONC benchmark
worked_example.setup: An illustrative district has 1,500,000 people. The deck's UN benchmark is at least five EmONC facilities per 500,000, of which at least one can do surgery and transfusion (CEmONC).
steps: Count is not enough: the 15 must be spread, so measure travel time in the worst season.
worked_example.answer: At least 15 EmONC facilities, of which at least 3 can do surgery and transfusion, spread across the district.

mistakes: Telling a 'low risk' woman she is safe, which gives false reassurance and can cause delay one.
Counting a facility as BEmONC because MgSO4 is on the shelf when no provider will give it.
Sending an eclamptic woman on referral without the first dose of magnesium sulphate.
Averaging readiness scores across components when one missing element means zero capability.

recall.q: How many signal functions define BEmONC and CEmONC?
recall.a: Seven for basic and nine for CEmONC.

recall.q: What counts as a signal function being present?
recall.a: It was performed in the last three months.

recall.q: What are the four steps of referral?
recall.a: Recognise and decide, stabilise, transport and communicate ahead (with records travelling with her).

recall.q: What do the alert and action lines on a partograph mean?
recall.a: Crossing the alert line means reassess and prepare to refer; crossing the action line means intervention is overdue.

recall.q: Which element is called the commonest blocker for a caesarean?
recall.a: The anaesthetist.

sections.title: Postnatal & Newborn Care
sections.big_idea: The first hours and weeks hold the highest risk and the thinnest care. **Mother and baby are one clinical unit** in this window.
in_plain_words: Care often stops at delivery, yet a large share of maternal and most newborn deaths occur after birth. Early discharge, bed pressure and unpaid postnatal contact keep this stage weak, and deaths at home never reach facility data. WHO recommends the first postnatal contact within 24 hours for every birth, facility or home.

PPH remains the main threat, and active management of the third stage (oxytocin within a minute, controlled cord traction, uterine massage) prevents most cases in about a minute. HBNC sends ASHAs to the home on a fixed schedule. Newborn danger signs include not feeding, fast breathing, fever or low temperature, lethargy and cord redness. Kangaroo Mother Care and breastfeeding in the first hour protect small babies. **Treat mother and newborn in one visit.**

events.what: Oxytocin; bag-and-mask if baby not breathing
Highest PPH risk; first postnatal contact
Home visits; most newborn deaths occur

key_terms.meaning: Active management of the third stage of labour, which prevents most PPH.
Home-Based Newborn Care: ASHA visits on a fixed schedule in six weeks.
Kangaroo Mother Care: skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding, early discharge.
The first minute after birth for bag-and-mask resuscitation.
Infection at the cord, a route to sepsis.
Anything given before the first breastfeed.

worked_example.title: Compare two NFHS rounds and count visits
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 figures: breastfeeding within one hour 41.8% then 50.1%; exclusive breastfeeding under six months 63.7% then 55.8%. The HBNC schedule for an institutional birth has six visits.
steps: Home-birth schedule adds a day-1 visit: 6 + 1 = 7 visits.
Read it plainly: one indicator improved and the other worsened, so quote both.
worked_example.answer: Early initiation gained 8.3 points while exclusive breastfeeding lost 7.9 points; the home-birth schedule has 7 visits.

mistakes: Discharging a woman within hours and counting the delivery as a success.
Reading HBNC record coverage as visits made, when recorded coverage runs ahead.
Treating low temperature in a newborn as less serious than fever, when it is the worse sign.
Leaving postpartum depression out of the postnatal protocol.

recall.q: When does WHO recommend the first postnatal contact?
recall.a: Within 24 hours, for facility and home births alike.

recall.q: What are the AMTSL steps?
recall.a: Oxytocin within one minute, controlled cord traction, uterine massage and observation.

recall.q: On which days does an ASHA visit after an institutional birth?
Name three newborn danger signs.
recall.a: Any three of: not feeding, fast or difficult breathing, fever or low temperature, lethargy or convulsions, cord redness or discharge.

recall.q: Why is KMC low-cost and powerful?
recall.a: The mother's body provides warmth and feeding that an incubator needs power for.

sections.title: Family Planning & Safe Abortion
sections.big_idea: Contraception prevents maternal deaths **without touching a labour room**, and safe abortion removes a whole direct cause. Choice has to be real.
in_plain_words: Family planning lowers maternal deaths by reducing unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions and the highest-risk pregnancies. Four patterns raise risk: too young (under 18), too close (under 24 months), too many (high parity) and too old (over 35). WHO recommends at least 24 months between a live birth and the next conception.

Unmet need means women who want to delay or avoid pregnancy and use no method. NFHS-6 shows 8.5% of currently married women, down from 9.4%, with high discontinuation. The modern approach is rights-based, with India's targets abolished in 1996 and the 2016 Devika Biswas ruling on consent. On abortion, the MTP Act framework (2021 amendment) sets limits by gestation, yet **legal does not yet mean reachable**.

diagram.caption: only family planning prevents all four

key_terms.meaning: Women who want to delay or avoid pregnancy and use no method.
Intrauterine contraceptive device: reversible, effective for up to ten years.
India's injectable contraceptive, effective for three months.
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act; the 2021 amendment widened access.
The law banning sex determination, separate from abortion law.
Abortion services including post-abortion contraception.

worked_example.title: Read the unmet-need trend
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: unmet need 9.4% of currently married women in NFHS-5 and 8.5% in NFHS-6. Take an illustrative group of 1,000 such women.
steps: Minimum spacing from WHO: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 years between a live birth and the next conception.
worked_example.answer: Unmet need fell 0.9 points, about 9.6%, leaving 85 of every 1,000 women with an unmet need.

mistakes: Pushing methods to meet numbers. Unmet need is a gap in the woman's own intention.
Counting a method as available because it is on a poster when the sub-centre has no stock.
Confusing the PCPNDT Act on sex determination with abortion law, which deters lawful care.
Sending a woman home after an abortion without contraception.

recall.q: What does the 'too close' pattern mean?
recall.a: Pregnancies spaced less than 24 months apart.

recall.q: When did India abolish method-specific targets?
What did the Supreme Court rule in Devika Biswas in 2016?
recall.a: It ordered the closure of sterilisation camps and set consent and care standards.

recall.q: What are the MTP Act gestational steps after 2021?
recall.a: One practitioner up to 20 weeks, two for 20 to 24 weeks in specified categories, and beyond 24 weeks only for substantial fetal abnormality.

recall.q: What happens to unsafe abortion where it is legal, available and safe?
recall.a: It effectively disappears as a cause of death.

sections.title: Social Determinants & Equity
sections.big_idea: Poverty, gender, caste, education and geography decide who reaches care in time. **Respectful care** keeps women coming back.
in_plain_words: Clinical causes are the how and social determinants the why. Each determinant acts on delay one or delay two before a clinician is involved. Adolescent pregnancy raises the risk of obstructed labour, eclampsia and preterm birth, and the legal age of marriage for women is 18. Anaemia is the accumulated record of a girl's life of undernutrition.

Cut every indicator by wealth quintile, caste and tribe, state, district and rural or remote status, because national averages hide the gaps. Women's autonomy works through delay one. Respectful maternity care covers dignity, consent, freedom from abuse, non-discrimination and a companion. **Obstetric violence turns delay three into delay one for the next woman**, which makes it a mortality issue.

key_terms.meaning: A social condition that shapes who gets care in time.
Splitting a figure by group or place to expose gaps.
India's programme to target the districts furthest behind.
Respectful maternity care: dignity, privacy, consent and choice.
Abuse, non-consented procedures, neglect or discrimination in childbirth care.
A person of the woman's choice with her in labour.

worked_example.title: Size the state gap and its toll
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's SRS 2019-21 range: Kerala near 20 and the highest-burden states above 150 per 100,000 live births. Take an illustrative district with 50,000 live births a year.
steps: Ratio of the highest to Kerala: 150 ÷ 20 = 7.5.
Extra deaths in the district each year at that gap: 50,000 ÷ 100,000 × 130 = 65.
Read it plainly: the same national law and schemes produce close to eight-fold different risks.
worked_example.answer: About 7.5 times the risk and 130 extra deaths per 100,000 births, or 65 a year in this district.

mistakes: Reporting only a state average, which is too coarse to direct resources.
Teaching danger signs without engaging the husband or mother-in-law who decides.
Treating respectful care as a soft extra when disrespect pushes women away from facilities.
Naming individuals after a mistreatment complaint without changing overcrowding and supervision.

recall.q: Which delays do social determinants act on?
recall.a: Delay one and delay two.

recall.q: What is the legal age of marriage for women in India?
recall.a: 18, under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006.

recall.q: What intervention does the deck say has the strongest evidence for delaying early pregnancy?
recall.a: Keeping girls in secondary school.

recall.q: Name two RMC standards.
recall.a: Any two of: dignity and privacy, consent, freedom from abuse, non-discrimination, companionship in labour.

recall.q: Why does disaggregation matter?
recall.a: A good national average can hide a poorest group left far behind.

sections.title: India's Programmes & Progress
sections.big_idea: Each scheme answered the failure the last one exposed. **The remaining deaths are the harder ones**, in quality, equity and the districts nobody reports on.
in_plain_words: The National Health Mission is the system, and JSY (2005), JSSK (2011), PMSMA (2016), LaQshya (2017) and SUMAN (2019) are its instruments. They moved from getting women in, to making it free, to antenatal quality, labour-room quality and dignity. The ASHA is the hinge of the system, paid per activity, so unincentivised tasks lapse first.

India's MMR fell from around 250 (2004-06) to around 113 (2016-18) to around 93 (2019-21), now below 100 but above the SDG 3.1 target of 70. Improvement was fastest in institutional delivery and slowest in postnatal contact, full ANC and the spread between states. Use several sources: SRS for mortality, NFHS for level and equity, HMIS for trend, MDSR for causation. **Where sources disagree, the disagreement is usually the finding.**

diagram.caption: each scheme answers the failure the previous one exposed

key_terms.meaning: National Health Mission, the umbrella system for maternal health schemes.
Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan: free monthly antenatal check-ups.
Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan: assured, free, respectful care.
Sample Registration System, the authoritative MMR source.
Health Management Information System: monthly facility data.
Facility quality certification, incentive-linked.

worked_example.title: How far has India's MMR fallen?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's SRS figures: around 250 in 2004-06 and around 93 in 2019-21, against the SDG 3.1 target of 70.
steps: Read it plainly: the decline is large, and the rest of it must come from the districts and groups the first wave missed.
worked_example.answer: A fall of 157 points, about 62.8%, with 23 points still to go to reach 70.

mistakes: Assessing a programme on HMIS alone, the source most exposed to reporting pressure.
Expecting another point of institutional delivery to save the marginal life. Readiness on the night shift matters more.
Treating certification as quality when facilities may prepare only for the assessment.
Quoting an SRS figure without its confidence interval, especially for small states.

recall.q: Which scheme came first and which last in the deck's chronology?
recall.a: JSY in 2005 first and SUMAN in 2019 last.

recall.q: What did MMR in India stand at in 2019-21?
recall.a: Around 93 per 100,000 live births.

recall.q: What does LaQshya target?
recall.a: Labour-room and maternity-OT quality, through assessed and certified standards.

recall.q: Why are ASHA unincentivised tasks the first to lapse?
recall.a: The incentive list is the job description in practice.

recall.q: What is each source best for?
recall.a: HMIS for trend, NFHS for level and equity, SRS for mortality, MDSR for causation.

notes.2: Eleven sections follow the story of a pregnancy: why mothers die, where the time is lost, how care is chained together, each stage of care, then family planning, equity and India's schemes. If you work in MEL, design or advocacy, **spend longest on sections 3 and 4**, as slide 10 advises.
notes.4: Learn the three terms as three windows: 42 days for a maternal death, 42 days to one year for a late maternal death, and any death in the window, accidents included, for pregnancy-related. The cutoff is a convention, so **check a country's definition** before comparing counts.
notes.5: Keep three measures apart by their denominators: live births for the MMR, women aged 15 to 49 for the rate, and a woman's reproductive life for lifetime risk. Two places can share an MMR and differ in lifetime risk through fertility. **Check the denominator** before you compare reports.
notes.6: This slide turns maternal death from a tragedy into a duty failure. Use the four rights as a checklist for a facility visit: reachable emergency care, equal treatment, information, consent and dignity. **Courts have treated denial of care as a breach of Article 21**, which makes the right justiciable.
notes.7: Two numbers carry SDG 3.1: a global target below 70 and a floor of 140 for every country, both by 2030. The table's last row shows a missing level, since nothing sets a sub-national floor. **Disaggregate by state and district yourself.** Slide 96 gives the current MMR.
notes.8: Read the table down: bleeding needs oxytocin, eclampsia needs magnesium sulphate, sepsis needs clean delivery and antibiotics, obstruction needs a timely caesarean. All the remedies are old and cheap. **The failure sits in the supply chain, the roster and the road**, so ask about delivery first.
notes.9: Maternal health maps inequality at every level: between regions, states (Kerala near 20, the highest-burden states above 150), districts and wealth quintiles. A woman in one state faces close to eight times the risk of a woman in another. **Make district-level data a habit.**
notes.10: Use the four questions in order: what was the clinical cause, where did the time go, which stage did she fall out of, and what is the state doing for whom. The first appears on a death certificate. **The middle two are where programmes can act**, so give them the most time.
notes.12: Split causes into direct (from the pregnancy or its treatment) and indirect (conditions the pregnancy worsens). As direct deaths fall, indirect causes such as anaemia take a larger share. **Anaemia rarely appears as the certified cause**, so attribution understates it. Read the final row on trends.
notes.13: Memorise the order of direct causes by approximate global share: haemorrhage about a quarter, hypertensive disorders roughly one in seven, sepsis one in ten, unsafe abortion close to one in twelve. The chart is illustrative. **Plan from your own death review data**, because shares vary widely by country.
notes.14: PPH is the time-critical cause: a woman can bleed to death in under two hours, faster than an ambulance covers 40 km of rural road. So the defence is **a uterotonic within one minute of birth**. Ask which uterotonic a facility stocks, since oxytocin needs a cold chain.
notes.15: Treat the table as a ladder: raised BP with protein in urine, then headache and visual changes, then convulsions. Magnesium sulphate is the drug on the top two rungs. The failure comes earlier, in **the BP cuff and the urine dipstick**, because pre-eclampsia is silent until it is severe.
notes.16: Learn the six cleans by body part and object: hands, delivery surface, blade, cord tie, cord stump, perineum. Sepsis is slower than haemorrhage, so it can appear on day three **after the woman has gone home**. Facility sepsis rates measure quality as well as hygiene.
notes.17: Pair each condition with its remedy: obstructed labour with a timely caesarean, unsafe abortion with legal, safe services. Both are concentrated among the young, the poor and the remote. The fistula note shows **a delayed caesarean can leave a social catastrophe** for the survivor.
notes.18: Anaemia kills by removing reserve: below 7.0 g/dL a routine blood loss becomes fatal, and a woman with an Hb of 6 has none. About 52% of pregnant women in India were anaemic in NFHS-5. **Look for anaemia in the background of deaths** certified as haemorrhage.
notes.19: Danger concentrates in hours, in labour and the first 24 hours, while services are organised in days. A woman discharged four hours after an uncomplicated delivery goes home into her most dangerous window. For a weak system, **an attendant at birth and a working referral** come first.
notes.21: Fix the three delays in the order of a journey: deciding, reaching, receiving. Each has a different owner: household and ASHA, district transport, facility managers. A programme that only trains clinicians works on delay three. **Ask which delay is killing women** before choosing a response.
notes.22: Use the picture as a map for any death review: complication, then three gates, then outcome. Each gate is a place to intervene. **Write the owner of each gate under it** (household, district transport, facility managers) so no delay is left without someone responsible.
notes.23: Delay one is a rational calculation under bad information: the cost is certain, the danger uncertain, and someone else decides. A poster rarely shifts it. **A trusted ASHA who has accompanied a neighbour** does more. The right column lists fixes, including respectful care.
notes.24: Judge delay two by what happened on the worst night of last year, since fleet size says little. The row to remember: **the second referral is the one that kills**, because a woman sent to a facility that cannot manage her has spent her margin. Night dispatch and free transport are the fixes.
notes.25: Delay three happens inside the facility: no doctor, no blood, no working theatre, stockouts and process delays. As institutional delivery rises, it matters more. **The anaesthetist is the classic single point of failure**: an obstetrician and a theatre with no anaesthetist on night duty offer a caesarean on paper.
notes.26: The model's gain is to turn a cause of death into a list of system failures with owners. Its warning is about sequencing: **fixing one delay can move deaths to another**. The slide's example is cash incentives after JSY delivering more women to labour rooms that were not ready.
notes.27: Match remedy to delay: ASHA outreach and JSY for deciding (its cash also eases transport, delay two), referral transport and JSSK for reaching, EmONC and quality programmes for receiving. Each instrument has a limit, shown in the last column. **Check that a scheme targets the delay actually killing women** in your district.
notes.28: Turn the table into a death review: when did the family notice, how long until they left, how long was the journey, how long from arrival to first treatment, what was missing. Timings are approximate but the sequence is reliable. **Keep reviews no-blame**, or deaths stop being reported.
notes.30: Think of the continuum as links over time and place, where a break anywhere puts mother and baby at risk. The key idea is that **women fall out at the handovers**, which coverage statistics do not count. Test it in your district by comparing four-visit ANC with postnatal contact within 48 hours.
notes.31: Memorise the four stages in order: antenatal, skilled birth, postnatal, newborn. Each manages a different risk in a different window, so none substitutes for another. Excellent antenatal care cannot make up for an unattended birth. This is **the argument against single-intervention programmes**.
notes.32: The continuum runs across time (no stage skipped) and across place (home and community linked to facilities). The two fail differently: a time gap needs outreach, a place gap needs transport and communication. **The Mother and Child Protection Card** links both, if providers write in it.
notes.33: Four stages at 80% coverage each can mean 80% of women got everything, or a large group got nothing, and the aggregates look the same. **Only name-based tracking separates the two**, which RCH and HMIS are designed to do. Ask for the continuum-completion rate.
notes.34: Learn the cadres by place: ASHA in the village, ANM at the sub-centre or HWC, staff nurse or SBA at PHC or CHC, medical officer, specialist at the district hospital. The ASHA is the only one without a salary. **Every added ASHA duty is unpaid work** on the busiest link.
notes.35: Use the tier table as a referral map: sub-centre or HWC, PHC for basic EmONC, CHC or FRU for the full level, district hospital. An FRU is a definition, and **a designated FRU without an anaesthetist is not one**. The UN benchmark is five EmONC facilities per 500,000 people.
notes.36: The payoff slide ties each stage to the deaths it removes. Because each stage removes a different class of death, the returns add up. Use residual deaths as a diagnostic: **deaths after discharge point to postnatal care, and deaths in labour point to readiness and referral**.
notes.38: ANC finds silent risks: raised BP, low haemoglobin, malpresentation, infections, gestational diabetes. Almost none produce symptoms a woman would report. A visit that records weight and hands over tablets is incomplete, since **the BP cuff, the haemoglobin test and the urine dipstick** are what the visit is for.
notes.39: Learn the 2016 shift as 4 to 8, and visit to contact. The first contact should come before 12 weeks, with contacts across all three trimesters. The wording matters: **a contact can be delivered by a community health worker**, which makes eight achievable where eight facility visits are not.
notes.40: Read the NFHS-5 table with a gap in mind: about 58% had four visits, around seven in ten registered in the first trimester, and a much smaller minority had full ANC. India moved women into facilities faster than it improved their care. **Ask for full ANC**, which needs every component.
notes.41: Teach danger signs against Delay 1: bleeding, severe headache and blurred vision, fever, swelling and convulsions, reduced movement or leaking fluid. Counsel the decision-maker as well as the woman, and **pair each sign with a rehearsed plan**: which facility, whose phone, whose vehicle, what money.
notes.42: Anaemia in India (NFHS-5): about 52% of pregnant women, 57% of all women and 67% of young children. The trend ran the wrong way despite a decade of supplementation. Iron deficiency is the largest contributor but **hookworm, malaria and sickle-cell and thalassaemia** need other responses.
notes.43: IFA works only if swallowed. The table lists why it fails (side effects, stopping early, stockouts, counting distribution as consumption) and what helps. **Track the tablets swallowed**, since distribution figures overstate. Anemia Mukt Bharat adds testing, deworming and fortified staples, which the slide reads as an admission.
notes.44: Tetanus is the success story: two doses of a cheap vaccine plus clean delivery eliminated neonatal tetanus as a public-health problem in India, validated in 2015. Elimination means under one case per 1,000 live births per district, so **the threshold has to be held** where immunisation slips.
notes.45: Use the right-hand table as an audit of one visit: BP, haemoglobin, urine protein, fetal growth, birth planning. Each drops out for a supply or staffing reason. That makes ANC quality **measurable through stock registers**, which beat attendance counts. PMSMA gives a fixed monthly day with a specialist.
notes.47: Learn the SBA definition: an accredited doctor, nurse or midwife who manages normal birth and can recognise, manage or refer complications. Training traditional birth attendants in the 1980s did not reduce maternal mortality. **Deaths need drugs, surgery and blood**, which training cannot supply.
notes.48: Institutional delivery is a strategy against delay. Read the table by row: a facility birth has already resolved delays 1 and 2, leaving only delay 3. It turns a two-hour problem into a two-minute one, **if the facility is ready**. Coverage and quality investment have to move together.
notes.49: Hold three NFHS figures: 39%, 79%, 89%, a rise of fifty points in fifteen years. The slide credits JSY, ASHAs and free entitlements. Gains are uneven: home births stay concentrated among the poorest quintile, Adivasi communities and remote blocks, **the groups with the highest mortality**.
notes.50: JSY, launched in 2005, pays eligible women cash for a facility birth, with an ASHA incentive for accompaniment and higher amounts in low-performing states. Evaluations credit it with much of the rise in facility births. **Remember its three criticisms**: payment delays, exclusion of women without documents, and silence on quality.
notes.51: Cash buys a journey and a decision. It cannot buy an anaesthetist, oxytocin in stock or respectful treatment. This is the general lesson: **conditional cash transfers work on the behaviour they pay for** and are silent on what follows. Once women arrive, supply is the binding constraint.
notes.52: JSSK removes the bill: free delivery including caesarean, drugs, diagnostics, blood, transport both ways and diet. It is only as strong as the woman's knowledge of it. **Display entitlements in the labour room in the local language**, and check this first on a facility visit.
notes.53: Remember the pair as pull and push: JSY pulls women in with cash, and JSSK makes sure it costs nothing once they arrive. One is demand-side conditional cash, the other a supply-side entitlement. **Together they address both the decision and the bill.**
notes.54: A facility birth saves a life only if the facility is ready. The table shows four quality questions hiding behind headline numbers: was a skilled provider present, is the labour room staffed each shift, is there an anaesthetist at night, was matched blood available. **India has largely won coverage and inherited quality.**
notes.56: Some complications cannot be predicted. Most women who develop one have no known risk factor, so every birth needs access to emergency care. **Risk screening misdirects resources** and reassures the wrong women. A 'low risk' label can itself produce delay one.
notes.57: BEmONC has seven signal functions at PHC level, and the full level (CEmONC) adds caesarean and transfusion for nine, needing a theatre, an anaesthetist and a blood bank. The UN benchmark is five facilities per 500,000, one of them able to do surgery and transfusion. **Spread matters**: five clustered in one town leave half the district out of reach.
notes.58: Learn the seven basic functions by what they treat: antibiotics for sepsis, uterotonics for haemorrhage, magnesium sulphate for eclampsia, manual removal and removal of retained products for retained tissue, assisted delivery and newborn resuscitation. **A function not performed in three months counts as absent.**
notes.59: Referral has four steps: recognise early, stabilise before moving, transport, and communicate ahead. **Pre-referral stabilisation is the step most often skipped**, and a first dose of magnesium sulphate protects an eclamptic woman on the journey. A referral without a phone call is a gamble on readiness.
notes.60: A partograph plots labour against time with alert and action lines. Crossing the alert line means reassess and prepare to refer, and crossing the action line means intervention is overdue. It makes **hours of nothing happening visible**. WHO's Labour Care Guide (2020) has since replaced the classic form.
notes.61: Read the partograph as a clock and a conscience on one page: it needs no electricity and catches obstructed labour before the uterus ruptures. Apply the two lines: alert means be warned, action means augment, refer or operate. **Check whether your labour rooms fill it in** during a shift.
notes.62: Learn the first-minute sequence: dry and keep warm, stimulate, clear the airway if needed, then bag-and-mask ventilation within the first minute. Skills decay without practice, so Helping Babies Breathe uses **regular low-dose refresher drills**. The same hands attend two lives, which links maternal and newborn survival.
notes.63: Readiness is five links: people, drugs, blood, theatre and transport. The slide's key sentence says readiness is a conjunction, and a sum would mislead. **Score a facility as ready as its weakest element on its worst shift**, because averaging across components hides the missing link.
notes.65: Postnatal care is the most dangerous and the most neglected part of the continuum. Early discharge, bed pressure and unpaid contact keep it weak, and **deaths at home never reach facility data**. WHO recommends the first postnatal contact within 24 hours for every birth. Strictly measured, India is weak here.
notes.66: Learn the windows: first 24 hours (highest PPH risk), first 48 hours, first week, six weeks. The HBNC schedule for an institutional birth starts on day 3, so days one and two depend on the woman still being in the facility. **Closing the gap means holding women 48 hours or visiting sooner.**
notes.67: PPH remains the top cause of postnatal maternal death, and active management of the third stage prevents most cases in about a minute: oxytocin within one minute, controlled cord traction, uterine massage, observation. This is the **highest-return single action** in the course. Eye estimates of blood loss are unreliable.
notes.68: HBNC sends ASHAs to the home on a fixed schedule in the first six weeks to check the mother, examine the newborn, watch a feed and refer. It catches deaths the facility misses. Because visits are incentive-paid and self-reported, **ask mothers** as well as reading the records.
notes.69: Memorise five newborn danger signs: not feeding, fast or difficult breathing, fever or low temperature, lethargy or convulsions, cord redness or discharge. Poor feeding is the earliest sign of sepsis. **Low temperature is the worse sign and alarms families less**, so counsel on it explicitly.
notes.70: KMC is skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding and early discharge with support. WHO now recommends starting it at birth for small and preterm babies. The barriers are institutional: wards that separate mother from baby. **Adopting KMC means changing the layout** so a mother can sit for days.
notes.71: Compare the two rounds: breastfeeding within an hour rose from 41.8% to 50.1%, while exclusive breastfeeding under six months fell from 63.7% to 55.8%. The first hour is decided by whoever attends the birth, so **it is a labour-room practice**. Caesarean, separation and prelacteal feeds are common reasons for missing it.
notes.72: Treat mother and baby as one clinical unit: one visit, one record, one referral decision. The package covers the mother's bleeding, BP, infection and mood and the newborn's weight, warmth, feeding and danger signs. **Postpartum depression belongs on the list** and is almost never screened for.
notes.74: Family planning lowers maternal deaths by cutting exposures: fewer unintended pregnancies, fewer unsafe abortions, better spacing and fewer high-risk ages. It is the one intervention in the course that **reduces the denominator**. Modelling shows meeting unmet need would avert a large share of remaining deaths.
notes.75: Use the four 'too' patterns as a screen: too young (under 18), too close (under 24 months), too many (high parity), too old (over 35). **Only contraception prevents all four**; obstetric care manages the consequences. WHO recommends at least 24 months between a live birth and the next conception.
notes.76: Unmet need is a gap in intention: women who want to delay or avoid pregnancy and use no method. The table pairs each reason with a supply or counselling fix. NFHS-6 gives 8.5% of currently married women, down from 9.4%. **Discontinuation stays high**, which coverage figures miss.
notes.77: The basket covers spacing, long-acting, permanent and emergency methods. The principle is informed choice, and **choice on a poster differs from choice at the sub-centre**, since every method must be in stock. India's mix leans heavily towards female sterilisation, reflecting programme history and provider incentives.
notes.78: The shift from targets to rights is the lesson: method targets for workers, sterilisation camps and counts of acceptors gave way to counselling quality, need met and choice honoured. India abolished method-specific targets in 1996, and Devika Biswas (2016) set consent standards. **Treat this as settled law.**
notes.79: Restricting abortion changes who performs it and under what conditions, and leaves the number of abortions where it was. The table shows the pattern: legal and available makes unsafe abortion disappear, restricted makes it a leading cause. **Medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol** needs a route to care if it fails.
notes.80: Remember the MTP ladder after 2021: one practitioner up to 20 weeks, two for 20 to 24 weeks in specified categories, beyond 24 weeks only for substantial fetal abnormality via a State Medical Board. The Act protects the provider, so **access depends on a provider's willingness**. PCPNDT is a separate law.
notes.81: A permissive law is necessary and still insufficient: too few trained and willing providers, fear of PCPNDT liability, stigma and low awareness keep unsafe abortion alive. The law changed in 1971 and access has lagged. **Full abortion care includes contraception afterwards**, or the woman returns in the same situation.
notes.83: Clinical causes are the how and social determinants the why. Poverty, gender norms, caste, education and geography act through cost, decision rights, treatment and distance, all on delay one or two. **A health system can compensate for these but cannot remove them**, so programmes should not over-promise.
notes.84: Adolescent pregnancy raises obstructed labour and fistula, eclampsia, preterm birth and delay in seeking care. The legal age of marriage for women is 18 (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006). **Keeping girls in secondary school** has the strongest evidence and sits entirely outside the health system.
notes.85: Read anaemia as the accumulated record of a life: girl child, adolescence, first pregnancy, between births. Supplementation that begins at antenatal registration treats the last few months of a twenty-year deficit. That is the case for **anaemia programmes in schools and for adolescent girls**.
notes.86: Cut every indicator by wealth quintile, caste and tribe, state, district and rural or remote status. The district is the unit where gaps become actionable, since state averages are too coarse. India's Aspirational Districts programme **targets the districts furthest behind**. Ask which women are still dying, and where.
notes.87: The chart is an illustrative pattern of skilled birth attendance by wealth group, so read its shape and leave its numbers out of reports. The lesson is that **a good national average can hide a poorest group left far behind**. Make disaggregation a default step in any dashboard you build.
notes.88: Women's autonomy works as a mechanism: no say in seeking care creates delay one, no control of money creates delays one and two, no unaccompanied travel creates delay two. Education, income and mobility **keep their effect in regressions after controlling for access to services**, because they change who can act and how fast.
notes.89: Respectful maternity care covers dignity and privacy, consent, freedom from abuse, non-discrimination and a companion in labour. A companion brings shorter labour and less intervention yet is refused in most Indian labour rooms as routine. **Measure RMC through exit interviews, consent records and companion presence.**
notes.90: Obstetric violence includes verbal abuse, non-consented procedures, neglect and demands for informal payment. A woman mistreated once may never return and may warn others. It **turns delay three into delay one for the next woman**. The drivers are structural: overcrowded labour rooms, exhausted staff and no supervision.
notes.92: NHM is the system and the schemes are its instruments. Learn five components: ASHA cadre, untied funds, Rogi Kalyan Samitis, JSSK entitlements and quality programmes. NHM made schemes fundable and staffable and created HMIS and name-based tracking, so **what can be counted is a policy choice made here**.
notes.93: Read the scheme map as a chronology: JSY 2005, JSSK 2011, PMSMA 2016, LaQshya 2017, SUMAN 2019. Each answers the failure the previous one exposed: coming, cost, antenatal quality, labour-room quality, dignity. The closing lesson for designers: **solving one constraint reveals the next**.
notes.94: ASHAs are the hinge of the system, paid per activity: pregnancy follow-up, accompaniment, HBNC visits, family planning counselling. The incentive list is the job description in practice, so unincentivised tasks such as postnatal counselling are **the first to lapse**. They remain classified as volunteers despite the WHO award in 2022.
notes.95: LaQshya sets standards for labour rooms and maternity OTs, SUMAN assures free, dignified care with a grievance route, MDSR reviews every death without blame, and Kayakalp and NQAS certify facilities. Certification has a known risk: **facilities prepare for the assessment**. Check standards on an unannounced night visit.
notes.96: Hold three MMR points: around 250 (2004-06), 113 (2016-18) and 93 (2019-21). India is below 100 and above the SDG 3.1 target of 70, which eight states have reached. SRS samples, so **each figure has a confidence interval** and small-state estimates are unstable.
notes.97: Sort the two columns: what improved fastest responds to coverage, and what has not responds to quality. The marginal life saved is unlikely to come from another point of institutional delivery. It comes from **readiness on the night shift** and the districts nobody reports on.
notes.98: Pair each indicator with its source and weakness: SRS for mortality (sampled, lagging), NFHS for level and equity (every five years, self-reported), HMIS for monthly trend (reporting pressure), MDSR for causation. **Triangulate**, and treat disagreement between sources as the finding.
notes.99: Use the table as a finding aid: SRS for MMR, NFHS fact sheets for coverage, MoHFW guidelines for entitlements, WHO for clinical standards, Thaddeus and Maine for the delays. For district work the **NFHS district fact sheets** are the most useful document. Check whether NFHS-6 district estimates exist.
